title: Contains Duplicate II
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every nearby pair versus a hash map of most recent indices.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return true if there are two distinct indices i and j such that nums[i] equals nums[j] and the absolute difference between i and j is at most k.

blocks.caption: Track each value's most recent index seen so far, checking the distance on every repeat

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return true if there are two distinct indices i and j such that nums[i] equals nums[j] and the absolute difference between i and j is at most k.

blocks.title: Analogy: Spotting a Repeat Visitor Within a Short Time Window
blocks.text: Like checking a sign in sheet for any name that appears twice within a limited number of entries of each other, rather than caring whether that name ever repeats anywhere at all in the whole sheet.

blocks.caption: Find any repeated value whose two occurrences are close enough together in the array

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["1 appears at indices 0 and 3, a distance of 3","exactly at the allowed limit","The absolute difference between indices 0 and 3 is exactly 3, which satisfies \"at most k\" when k is 3"],["Answer","true","A pair of equal values exists whose index distance does not exceed k"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["1 appears at indices 2 and 3, a distance of 1","within the allowed limit","Indices 2 and 3 are adjacent, a distance of 1, which satisfies \"at most k\" when k is 1"],["Answer","true","At least one valid nearby duplicate pair exists"]]}

blocks.text: Every repeated value here (1, 2, and 3) is exactly 3 apart, further than the allowed distance of 2, so the answer is false.
Before checking pairs directly, notice that only one piece of information about a value's history ever matters at any point: where did it most recently appear, not every place it has ever appeared.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If a value repeats several times in the array, the gap between two consecutive occurrences is always smaller than or equal to the gap between occurrences that are further apart, so the most recent prior occurrence is always the best, smallest-distance, candidate to compare against.

Observation 2: This means there is never a need to remember every past index a value appeared at; remembering just the single most recent one is always sufficient to correctly answer the distance question.

Observation 3: A hash map from value to its most recent index gives an O(1) lookup for "was this value seen before, and if so, how far back", replacing a scan of up to k positions with a single map access.

Observation 4: Every value's recorded index must be updated after each check, even when the check fails, since a later occurrence of that value should compare against this occurrence, not some even older one.

Whenever only the nearest prior occurrence of something matters, not its full history, a single hash map tracking "most recent index seen" turns a windowed pairwise scan into one linear pass.

This same "only the most recent matters" insight is what makes many nearby-duplicate and sliding-window-adjacent problems solvable in O(n), once it is recognized that older occurrences are strictly dominated by newer ones for this specific kind of distance check.
Check every pair of indices within distance k of each other directly, comparing their values.

items: For every index i, check every index j within k positions after it.
If nums[i] equals nums[j], a valid duplicate has been found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop's upper bound, min(i + k, n - 1), stops the search from ever looking beyond either k positions ahead or the actual end of the array, whichever comes first.
The inner loop starts at j = i + 1, never checking index i against itself, since the problem requires two distinct indices.
The function returns true the instant any qualifying pair is found, since only the existence of one such pair matters, not how many exist.

blocks.text: Every pair within the allowed distance is directly checked, so any valid nearby duplicate is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times k), checking up to k positions ahead for every index.
Space: O(1) extra, no additional structure is used.
Limitation: for a large k, this approaches O(n squared), when tracking each value's most recent position seen so far could answer the same question in a single linear pass.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's cost comes directly from re-scanning up to k positions ahead for every single index, repeating a very similar check over and over as the window slides forward by one each time. But the actual question at each index, "does this value already appear within the last k positions", does not need to re-derive an entire nearby window from scratch, it only needs one fact: where did this exact value last appear, if at all? A hash map keyed by value, storing the most recently seen index, answers that in O(1), replacing an up-to-k-length inner scan with a single lookup and a single arithmetic comparison. The map is updated after every check, always keeping the most recent index for each value, since that is the only occurrence that could ever be the closest match for a future repeat.

Keep a hash map from value to the most recent index it was seen at. Walk through the array once; for each value, if it has been seen before, check whether the current index minus that recorded index is at most k. Either way, update the map with the current index, since only the most recent occurrence of a value can ever matter for future comparisons.
A hash map tracking each value's most recent index, checked and updated in a single pass.

blocks.caption: Optimized: track each value's most recent index, check the distance on every repeat

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant time average map operations.
Space: O(min(n, number of distinct values)), for the map of most recent indices.

Because last_seen always holds the most recent index for each value, the moment a repeat is found, the distance being checked is automatically the smallest possible distance to any earlier occurrence of that value. If even that closest occurrence fails the distance check, every other, more distant occurrence of the same value would fail it too, so checking only the most recent one is not just convenient, it is provably sufficient to catch every valid nearby duplicate.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Conclusion"],"rows":[["Current index minus last seen index is at most k","A valid nearby duplicate exists; return true immediately"],["Current index minus last seen index is more than k","This particular pair does not qualify, but the index is still updated in case a closer repeat appears later"]]}

items: enumerate(nums), or the indexed for loop, gives both the value and its index together, since both are needed simultaneously for the distance check.
The lookup and distance check happens before any update to the map, so the comparison always uses the prior recorded index, not the current one.
last_seen[num] = i runs unconditionally after the check, whether or not a match was found, since this index must become the new "most recent" reference for any future occurrence of this value.
The function returns false only after the entire array has been scanned without any qualifying pair ever being found, confirming no valid nearby duplicate exists anywhere.

blocks.text: Tracking only the most recent occurrence of each value, rather than every occurrence, is the key simplification here, since only the closest prior repeat could ever satisfy the distance constraint.

items: Storing every past index of a value in a list and checking all of them, when only the single most recent one is ever relevant, which wastes both time and memory.
Forgetting to update the recorded index for a value even when the current check fails, which would cause a stale, too-far-back index to incorrectly be used in a future comparison.
Confusing the distance constraint's direction, checking for a distance strictly less than k instead of at most k, which incorrectly rejects pairs exactly at the allowed limit.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["k equal to 0","Only truly identical indices could ever match, which is never true since i and j must be distinct, so the answer is always false"],["k large enough to cover the entire array","Reduces to simply checking whether any duplicate value exists at all, regardless of position"]]}

items: Mention the alternative sliding window hash set approach, maintaining a set of the last k elements, adding the new one and removing the one that falls out of range, as an equally valid technique with the same asymptotic complexity.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Duplicate values within a distance or window constraint" points toward tracking the most recent index, or maintaining a sliding window set, per value, instead of rescanning a window for every position.

items: How would you solve Contains Duplicate III, which also bounds how close in value, not just index, two elements must be? A sliding window combined with a sorted structure, like a balanced BST or bucket-based approach, is needed, since a plain hash map can no longer answer "is there a value within a numeric range" in O(1).

What if k could be negative or the array could be empty? A negative k would make the distance condition impossible to satisfy, always false, and an empty array trivially also returns false, both handled naturally without special-casing since the loop simply would not execute meaningfully.

Could this be solved with a sliding window of a hash set instead of a hash map of indices? Yes: maintain a set of the last k elements, checking for membership before adding the new element and removing the element that falls out of the window, an equally valid O(n) alternative.
Same "track only the most recent relevant occurrence" insight as many sliding-window and nearest-neighbor style array problems.
Same hash-map-based single-pass technique as Two Sum and the simpler, no-distance-constraint version of Contains Duplicate.
Directly extends into Contains Duplicate III, which adds a value-closeness constraint on top of this problem's index-closeness constraint.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n times k) time, O(1) space.
Optimized: O(n) time, O(min(n, distinct values)) space.

items: Pattern: Hash map tracking each value's most recent index, checked in a single pass
Core Idea: Only the closest prior occurrence of a repeated value can ever satisfy a distance constraint, so tracking just the most recent index per value is always sufficient
Time: O(n)
Space: O(min(n, distinct values))
Most Important Observation: When only the nearest prior occurrence of something matters, a single hash map replaces an entire windowed rescan
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Remember only the last place you saw it
